title: Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS)
summary: Gives practical recommendations for configuring and using TLS and DTLS securely, written after several serious attacks on these protocols and their common cipher suites came to light. It covers protocol versions, cipher choices and related settings that help avoid known weaknesses. It was replaced by RFC 9325.

eli5.summary: A safety checklist for locking the doors on your internet connections: which locks are weak, which are strong, and how to set them up so burglars cannot easily get in.

subtitle: The 2015 best-current-practice checklist for configuring TLS 1.2 and DTLS safely, since replaced by RFC 9325.

tldr.problem: Several serious attacks on TLS emerged, including attacks on its most common cipher suites such as AES-CBC and RC4, so deployers needed updated guidance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives minimum recommendations: drop SSLv2 and SSLv3, require TLS 1.2, disable RC4, NULL and export ciphers, prefer forward-secret AEAD suites, and avoid risky features such as TLS compression.
tldr.outcome: It was a point-in-time Best Current Practice and is now obsoleted by RFC 9325, which should be used instead.

today: RFC 7525 has been obsoleted by RFC 9325, and is also updated by RFC 8996. Use the newer RFC for current guidance. The text itself says it is a point-in-time statement that is likely to be updated once TLS 1.3 is noticeably deployed.

sections.title: Why These Recommendations Exist
sections.content:
TLS and DTLS protect application protocols such as HTTP, SMTP, IMAP, POP, SIP and XMPP. Over a few years, serious attacks emerged, including attacks on AES-CBC and RC4, which together had been the most widely deployed ciphers. A companion document, RFC 7457, describes the attacks in detail.

This document is a floor, not a ceiling: minimum recommendations for the vast majority of deployments, with stronger options always allowed. Unless stated otherwise, each applies to both TLS and DTLS. It applies to TLS 1.2 and earlier, and readers should not assume it applies to any future TLS version. It also warns that a security BCP is a point-in-time statement.
sections.eli5: Some of the old locks on the internet's doors got picked by burglars. This list says which locks to throw away and which to buy.

sections.title: Protocol Versions and Connection Handling
sections.content:
On versions, implementations MUST NOT negotiate SSL 2 or SSL 3, and SHOULD NOT negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 unless no higher version is available. They MUST support TLS 1.2 and MUST prefer it. For DTLS, they SHOULD NOT negotiate DTLS 1.0, and MUST support and prefer DTLS 1.2. Clients that fall back after a server rejects a higher version MUST NOT fall back to SSLv3 or earlier, because a man-in-the-middle can force fallback.

Other general rules cover connection handling:

  • Strict TLS: prefer strict TLS over dynamic upgrade such as STARTTLS to resist SSL Stripping. HTTP implementations MUST support HSTS, and web servers SHOULD use it.
  • Compression: TLS-level compression SHOULD be disabled because of attacks such as CRIME.
  • Session tickets: resumption data MUST be authenticated and encrypted with a strong cipher, ticket keys MUST be changed regularly (for example once every week), and ticket validity SHOULD be limited.
  • Renegotiation: where implemented, both sides MUST implement the renegotiation_info extension.
  • SNI: implementations MUST support Server Name Indication where higher protocols such as HTTPS benefit from it.
sections.eli5: Use the newest door lock, never go back to the oldest ones, and keep your spare keys changed often.

sections.title: Cipher Suite Recommendations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT negotiate NULL-encryption suites or RC4 suites, and MUST NOT negotiate suites offering less than 112 bits of security, including export-level encryption. They SHOULD NOT negotiate suites under 128 bits of security, and SHOULD NOT use RSA key transport ("static RSA") because it has no forward secrecy. They MUST support and prefer suites with forward secrecy, meaning the DHE and ECDHE families.

The RECOMMENDED suites, all TLS 1.2-only AEAD suites, are TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. Clients SHOULD offer TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 first, and servers MUST prefer it over weaker suites.

On key sizes, DH keys of at least 2048 bits are RECOMMENDED, elliptic curves of less than 192 bits SHOULD NOT be used, and RSA server certificates SHOULD have at least a 2048-bit modulus. Implementations MUST NOT use the Truncated HMAC extension.
sections.eli5: Pick locks that cannot be copied after the fact, throw away the flimsy ones, and make the keys long enough that nobody can guess them.

sections.title: Who This Applies To
sections.content:
The recommendations target common uses of TLS and DTLS: web, email (IMAP, POP3, SMTP), instant messaging (XMPP, IRC) and real-time media using SRTP with DTLS. They assume the goals of confidentiality, data integrity and authentication.

The RFC does not change mandatory-to-implement cipher suites set by existing application protocols; those protocols must explicitly update their own definitions. Designers of new protocols are expected to conform unless they document compelling reasons. Opportunistic security, where TLS use is optional, is out of scope, since strict adherence could cause fallback to cleartext, which is worse.
sections.eli5: The checklist is for normal everyday doors that need to be both private and trustworthy, not for special cases like doors that are meant to stay open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The broader considerations include:

  • Host name validation: some TLS implementations do not validate host names, so application authors may need their own validation. A host name found through an insecure DNS query SHOULD NOT be used as a reference identifier.
  • Forward secrecy: it protects recorded conversations if long-term keys are later compromised, and the RFC advocates strict use of forward-secrecy-only ciphers.
  • DH exponent reuse: reusing exponents for more than a few hours can negate forward secrecy.
  • Certificate revocation: no complete and efficient solution exists. CRLs have scaling problems, clients typically soft-fail on OCSP, and OCSP stapling is ineffective against a MITM that ignores the request. Servers SHOULD support OCSP and the status_request and status_request_v2 extensions.
sections.eli5: Even the best lock fails if you do not check who is at the door, and a stolen key must not open yesterday's mail as well.
